summary: Capstone for early fractions (ages 7-8): given a word problem, the child must recognise WHICH fraction idea it calls for (finding a fraction of a quantity, comparing/ordering, equivalence, or adding/subtracting), choose a method, carry it out, and judge whether the answer is reasonable. The object of learning is the disposition of a strategic problem-solver — sense-making before calculating, monitoring progress, and checking plausibility — developed through rich, varied, non-routine problems, worked examples that model strategy SELECTION (not just execution), and talk that makes reasoning audible. Recognition-before-calculation is the core skill; key-word matching ('altogether' → add) is the central trap to dismantle.
misconceptions: Key-word matching: latches onto a surface word ('altogether', 'left') and applies the associated operation regardless of the problem's meaning
Applies the most recently taught procedure to every problem regardless of what it asks
Calculates without a plan and never checks whether the answer is plausible
Cannot start a problem unless the operation is explicitly stated ('but it doesn't tell me to divide')

activities.title: Solve it WITH a mentor who never gives the method
steps: Work through a mixed bag of fraction word problems with a partner or in-role mentor (a teacher, another child, or a Socratic tutor character) who reads each problem aloud.
Before doing any arithmetic, say out loud what KIND of problem this is — find-a-fraction-of, compare/order, equivalence, or add/subtract — and HOW you can tell from the situation.
Talk through a plan (what will you do first, and why) before calculating.

When the mentor deliberately offers a tempting key word ('it says altogether, so we add?'), decide whether that word really fits the situation or whether the problem is actually about something else (e.g. finding 1/4 of a set).
After getting an answer, check it makes sense ('could 3/4 of 12 be more than 12?') every single time.
activities.insight: Recognising what a problem is really asking — and checking whether an answer is plausible — is the skill, not the arithmetic. The habit becomes owned when the child hears themselves catch a key-word trap and reason from the situation's structure instead.

activities.title: Sort-then-model workspace: tag the problem, build a model, then answer
steps: For each word problem, first TAG it by type: fraction-of, compare, equivalence, or add/subtract.
Build a bar/strip model — or a double number line for fraction-of and comparison problems — of the situation to show the quantities and relationships BEFORE choosing an operation.
Use the model structure to decide what to do, then calculate.
Pass a 'does this make sense?' check before submitting your answer.
activities.insight: Externalising the plan-then-do structure — tag, model, then calculate — forces the recognition step and makes the situation's structure (not a key word) the basis for choosing an operation.

activities.title: Mixed problem set that discourages key-word matching
steps: Work a mixed set of varied fraction word problems, first categorising each by type.
For problems presented as multiple choice, pick the answer, then check whether your choice came from the situation's structure or from a surface word.
Where possible, write or say why the chosen type fits the situation, not just which answer you picked.
activities.insight: Across varied surface features, the underlying structure determines the method; options that reward key-word matching or last-procedure-applied reveal when a child is pattern-matching instead of reasoning.

activities.title: Model the planning, not just the answer (worked and partial examples)
steps: Study worked and partially-worked examples that show understand → plan → do → check, with the CHOICE of strategy made visible ('this is a fraction-of problem because...').
Fill in a visible problem-solving frame (understand → plan → do → check) for new problems, completing missing steps in partially-worked examples.
Include at least some problems with no stated operation and some multi-step problems, so you practise imposing structure yourself.
activities.insight: Expert problem-solving has explicit phases — planning and looking-back are as important as execution. Separating the choice of strategy from its execution makes the strategic step learnable rather than assumed.

checkQuestion: I'm going to give you three different fraction problems, one at a time. Before you work any of them out, just tell me: what kind of problem is this, and what would you do first? Then we'll talk about how you'd know if your answer makes sense.
checkAnswer: There is no single right answer to score — the aim is to surface HOW the child decides what a problem is asking and how they judge an answer. A strong response recognises each problem's underlying structure (this is a find-a-fraction-of problem; this is a compare/order problem), states a sensible first step and why, and offers a plausibility check ('the answer should be smaller than the whole').
